concepts.label: Water
concepts.note: Core vocabulary: inherited almost everywhere, and among the last words a language gives up to borrowing.

concepts.label: Mother
concepts.note: The mama pattern — a nasal plus an open vowel — recurs across wholly unrelated families. Jakobson put it down to infant babbling rather than common descent.

concepts.label: Hand
concepts.note: Plenty of languages use one word for hand and arm: Russian ruka and Tibetan lag-pa cover both.

concepts.label: Night
concepts.note: Old and stable. In the Indo-European test, nuit, Nacht, natt, noc, naktis and nychta are all the same word wearing different clothes.

concepts.label: Bread
concepts.note: The borrowing showcase. Japanese pan and Korean ppang both arrive from Portuguese pao.

concepts.label: Milk
concepts.note: Often a compound rather than a root: Mandarin niunai is literally cow-milk, Khmer tuk dos ko is cow-udder-water.

concepts.label: Star
concepts.note: Indo-European keeps a shared root here — Greek asteri, Armenian astgh and Hindi tara all go back to it.

concepts.label: Smoke
concepts.note: Frequently built out of the word for fire: Burmese mi-kho is fire-smoke.

concepts.label: Honey
concepts.note: Indo-European had two words for it. One, melit, gave Greek meli and Latin mel; the other, medhu, gave Sanskrit madhu, English mead and Tocharian mit — and Chinese mi has long been argued to be a loan from that last one.

concepts.label: Ash
concepts.note: Basic enough for the Swadesh list, yet rare in ordinary speech — the hardest row in the table.
